about: The institution narrative and the consecration of the bread. One clause of the Canon answers to no account of the Last Supper: elevátis óculis in cælum, with his eyes raised to heaven. The Gospels give that detail at the multiplication of the loaves, not in the upper room. From the consecration onward the priest does not separate his thumbs and forefingers until the ablutions. The words of consecration are set here in capitals, as both witnesses and every hand missal set them.

s02.translation: Who, the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy and venerable hands,

s03.narrative: The priest raises his eyes to heaven.

s04.translation: and lifting up his eyes to heaven, to thee, God, his almighty Father, giving thanks to thee, he blessed, broke and gave to his disciples, saying:

s05.translation: Take and eat of this, all of you.

s06.narrative: The priest holds the host with both hands between his forefingers and thumbs and speaks the words of consecration silently, distinctly and attentively over it, and over all the hosts together if there are more to be consecrated.

s08.narrative: The words spoken, the priest genuflects and adores the consecrated host, rises, shows it to the people, lays it on the corporal and genuflects again.

w001.function: The relative reaches back to Jesus Christ, named at the end of the prayer before.

w002.function: A word from the Roman calendar: prídie Kaléndas, the day before the first of the month.

w003.function: After prídie Latin puts quam — earlier than — where English says before.

w004.function: A deponent in the subjunctive: passive in form, active in meaning.

w011.function: Manus is 4th declension: singular and plural sound alike in the accusative, and the adjectives decide.

w014.function: An ablative absolute: a participle and a noun in the ablative form a clause of their own, with no grammatical link to the rest.

w015.function: This detail stands in no account of the Last Supper: the Gospels give it at the multiplication of the loaves.

w019.function: The Canon does not stop addressing the Father even while it narrates: “to thee” speaks to the one who hears the prayer.

w026.function: The participle agrees with the subject, Christ; it renders the Greek eucharistésas, from which the Eucharist takes its name.

w029.function: Three perfects in a row, with no connective but the -que attached to the last.

w030.function: From díscere, to learn; a disciple is a learner, not a follower.

w035.function: Mandúco is the colloquial word — to chew, not the polite édere; biblical Latin chose it, and the Romance languages kept it.

w038.function: Nominative, not vocative: it agrees with the unstated subject of the two imperatives — you all. The two forms sound alike.

w041.function: Enim never stands first in its clause; Latin slips it into second or third place.
